content: Write a cover letter for a school administrator job.

# Cover Letter — School Administrator

**[Your Name]**
[Street Address] | [City, State ZIP]
[Phone] | [Email] | [LinkedIn, if applicable]

[Date]

[Hiring Manager Name]
[Title, e.g., Superintendent / Director of Human Resources]
[School or District Name]
[Address]

Dear [Mr./Ms./Dr. Last Name],

I am writing to apply for the [Assistant Principal / Principal / Dean of Students] position at [School Name], as advertised on [where you found the posting]. With [X] years in education—including [X] years as a classroom teacher and [X] years in school leadership—I have built my career around a simple conviction: schools succeed when instruction is strong, expectations are clear, and every adult in the building feels supported in doing their best work. [School Name]'s commitment to [specific program, mission element, or initiative] is exactly the kind of work I want to help lead.

In my current role as [Your Title] at [Current School], I supervise [number] faculty members across [grade levels or departments] and oversee [key responsibilities: curriculum, scheduling, MTSS, discipline, etc.]. Some outcomes I'm proud of:

- **Instructional growth:** Redesigned our teacher observation and coaching cycle, contributing to a [X]% increase in [state assessment proficiency / student growth percentile] in [subject] over [timeframe].
- **Culture and climate:** Implemented [restorative practices / PBIS / a tiered behavior system], reducing out-of-school suspensions by [X]% while improving attendance from [X]% to [X]%.
- **Staff development:** Built and led a [mentorship program / PLC structure] that supported [number] new teachers, with [X]% retention into their second and third years.
- **Family engagement:** Increased conference participation by [X]% through [specific strategy, e.g., flexible scheduling, translated communications, home visits].

I lead by being visible and present—in classrooms, hallways, and at dismissal. I believe difficult conversations with staff should be frequent, honest, and grounded in evidence, and that discipline should be consistent without being rigid. I have also learned that the operational side of the job matters enormously: a master schedule that protects intervention time, a budget aligned to instructional priorities, and clear systems that spare teachers from unnecessary friction.

What draws me specifically to [School Name] is [one or two genuine, researched details: a turnaround effort, a demographic you have experience serving, a dual-language program, a new strategic plan, the district's approach to literacy, etc.]. My experience with [relevant experience] would allow me to contribute to that work immediately.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience aligns with your needs, and I'm happy to provide references from supervisors, colleagues, and families. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

**[Your Name]**
[Credentials, e.g., M.Ed., Administrative License #12345]

---

### Tips for customizing this

- **Replace every bracket** and cut anything that doesn't apply—a shorter, honest letter beats a padded one.
- **Use real numbers** wherever possible. Search committees read dozens of letters that say "improved student outcomes"; the ones with data stand out.
- **Name the school specifically** in paragraph one and four. Reviewers can spot a mass-mailed letter instantly.
- **Keep it to one page** (roughly 350–450 words once you trim).
- **Mirror the posting's language.** If the job description emphasizes "instructional leadership" or "equity-centered practices," use those phrases where they honestly describe your work.
- **Check your license status** is stated clearly if the role requires certification.

If you tell me the specific role, the school or district, and a few of your own accomplishments, I can tailor this into a finished draft.
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

# Cover Letter — School Administrator (Internal / Known Candidate)

I've written this for the version of the reader who has already watched you work: a superintendent, principal, or HR director in your own district who knows your record and doesn't need it recited. The letter therefore spends almost no time on background and almost all of it on what you would actually do in the role.

---

**[Your Name]**
[Phone] | [Email]

[Date]

Dear [Dr./Ms./Mr. Last Name],

I'm writing to formally put my name forward for the [Assistant Principal / Principal] position at [School Name].

You already know my work, so I won't restate it. I'd rather use this letter to tell you what I'd do in the first year.

**Instruction.** My read is that our biggest gap isn't teacher effort—it's the inconsistency between classrooms in [subject/grade band]. I'd tighten the observation cycle to short, frequent visits with same-week feedback, and I'd protect PLC time for looking at student work rather than logistics. Concretely: [specific first move, e.g., a common formative assessment in K–2 literacy by October].

**Culture.** [Name the real problem, e.g., "Referrals from the 7th-grade hallway are running well above the rest of the building."] I'd start by getting clear on whether that's a systems issue or a staffing one before changing any policy. My instinct is that we need a clearer tiered response and better follow-through on Tier 2, not a stricter code of conduct.

**Staff.** We're losing too many teachers in years two and three. I'd formalize the mentoring that currently happens by accident, and I'd make retention conversations a spring priority rather than an August surprise.

**Operations.** The master schedule is a values document. I'd build next year's around protected intervention time and common planning, and I'd be candid with you early about what that costs elsewhere.

Two things you should weigh honestly. First, [name a genuine gap—e.g., "my budget experience is limited to department-level; I'd need real support in year one"]. Second, moving me out of [current role] leaves a hole in [area], and I'd want us to have a plan for that before anything is announced.

I know this building and these families, and I think that's an argument for me rather than against—provided I'm willing to change things, which I am. I'd welcome the chance to talk it through.

Sincerely,

**[Your Name]**

---

### What changed and why

- **No credential recap, no mission-statement flattery.** Both read as padding to someone who already knows you and wrote the mission statement.
- **Past tense became future tense.** When the reader knows your track record, the open question isn't "what have you done?" but "what would you do with more authority?"
- **Specific diagnoses of the school's actual problems.** This is the biggest advantage an internal candidate has—use it. It also signals you'd arrive with judgment, not just enthusiasm.
- **Named a real weakness and a real cost.** With an external reader this can sink you. With someone who already knows your limitations, pretending they don't exist costs you credibility.
- **Much shorter.** Roughly 350 words. Familiar readers skim.

One caution: if the posting goes to a committee that includes outsiders—board members, parent reps, a neighboring principal—assume at least one reader doesn't know you, and add two sentences of grounding at the top.
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

# Cover Letter — School Administrator (Short Version)

Roughly 175 words, built for an email body, an application text field, or any placement where the reader sees the first two lines and decides whether to read the rest. The ask moves to sentence one; the diagnosis leads the body.

---

**Subject: [Your Name] — Candidate for [Assistant Principal], [School Name]**

Dear [Dr./Ms./Mr. Last Name],

I'm applying for the [Assistant Principal] position at [School Name]. You know my work, so here's what I'd do with the role.

Our gap isn't teacher effort—it's inconsistency between classrooms in [subject/grade band]. I'd move to short, frequent observations with same-week feedback, and protect PLC time for student work instead of logistics. First concrete step: [e.g., common formative assessment in K–2 literacy by October].

Second priority is retention. We're losing teachers in years two and three. I'd formalize the mentoring that currently happens by accident and start retention conversations in spring, not August.

One honest caveat: [genuine gap, e.g., my budget experience is department-level and I'd need support in year one]. And moving me out of [current role] leaves a hole in [area] worth planning for before any announcement.

Happy to talk it through whenever useful.

**[Your Name]** | [Phone]

---

### What I cut

- **Culture and operations sections.** Two priorities land harder than four in a short format. Save the master-schedule argument for the interview.
- **The closing paragraph about knowing the building.** Implied by the diagnosis itself—showing beats saying.
- **Hedging and connective tissue.** "I'd rather use this letter to…" is a sentence about the letter, not about the job.

**Kept deliberately:** the caveat and the succession note. They're short, and dropping them would make the letter read as a pitch rather than a straight conversation with someone who knows you.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

# Cover Letter — School Administrator (Short Version, Results Claim Removed)

Same letter, one sentence gone. Everything else is untouched.

---

**Subject: [Your Name] — Candidate for [Assistant Principal], [School Name]**

Dear [Dr./Ms./Mr. Last Name],

I'm applying for the [Assistant Principal] position at [School Name]. You know my work, so here's what I'd do with the role.

Our gap isn't teacher effort—it's inconsistency between classrooms in [subject/grade band]. I'd move to short, frequent observations with same-week feedback, and protect PLC time for student work instead of logistics. First concrete step: [e.g., common formative assessment in K–2 literacy by October].

Second priority is retention. I'd formalize the mentoring that currently happens by accident and start retention conversations in spring, not August.

One honest caveat: [genuine gap, e.g., my budget experience is department-level and I'd need support in year one]. And moving me out of [current role] leaves a hole in [area] worth planning for before any announcement.

Happy to talk it through whenever useful.

**[Your Name]** | [Phone]

---

### What I removed

The sentence "We're losing teachers in years two and three." It was the only outcome claim left in the draft, and it asserted a specific pattern in the school's results.

The retention paragraph still works without it—the proposals stand on their own as priorities rather than as fixes for a stated problem, and the tone doesn't change.

**One check:** if the claim you meant was actually the diagnostic line, "Our gap isn't teacher effort—it's inconsistency between classrooms," say so and I'll pull that instead. That paragraph would need a replacement opener, since the rest of it hangs off that premise.
